CFR asked members of the Society for Historians of American Foreign Relations what they considered to be the best and worst foreign policy decisions in U.S. history.

A U.S. Air Force surveillance flight over Cuba in October 1962 turned up evidence of what U.S. officials had feared: the Soviet Union was installing nuclear-armed missiles on the island. The discovery triggered a 13-day crisis, beginning on October 16, that brought the world to the brink of nuclear war.

Worried about escalation, President John F. Kennedy pursued backchannel communications with Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev that ended the crisis and led to several agreements that opened the door to the arms-control era.

Surveyed historians ranked Kennedy’s handling of the Cuban Missile Crisis as the tenth-best U.S. foreign policy decision.

The fact that the bond market (or for that matter just about everyone except the narrow set of AI investors) has never believed in the productivity-raising impact of AI at least in aggregate cuts both ways. 

If in the coming months AI adoption accelerates and/or evidence of agg productivity starts showing up, we could experience a right-tail risk or a massive melt-up of the AI trade. Ofc if the pace of adoption or frontier lab economics disappoint, left-tail risk is real as well. 

But at this point the expectation for a repeat of the dot-com style crash at some point over the next 18 months feels to have become increasingly the consensus. I’ve rarely met anyone who doesn’t think this is just a capex bubble and the only thing to do is to get out before the music stops sometime next year.
